title: Ulyana and the Postcards
premise: Freya Brightwater, a translator who has spent decades smoothing herself into other people's words, returns to her late grandmother's crumbling house in the coastal town of Vellamouth to prepare it for sale. Behind a wardrobe she finds a box of undelivered postcards—her grandmother Ulyana's letters, written over forty years to a sister who died young, and to Freya's estranged mother, never sent. As Freya translates the postcards, she uncovers the family's buried history: a fortune quietly stolen from a business partner, a daughter exiled for telling the truth, and Ulyana's own complicity in the silence. When the buyer's lawyer demands the house be cleared by month's end, Freya must choose between protecting the family myth that kept her safe and delivering the letters—and the truth they carry—to the living. She reads the final postcard aloud at the house's empty doorway, says goodbye to Ulyana in their dying language, and mails the rest, choosing truth over loyalty and finding, in the town's small responses, the first stirrings of a family she chose herself.
about_author: Xanthe Ravensworth is the pen name of a former court interpreter who spent eleven years listening to other people's truths before beginning to write her own. Her short fiction has appeared in several small literary journals, and 'Ulyana and the Postcards' is her first novel.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Freya arrives in Vellamouth to catalog the house for sale, fluent in three languages but losing the fourth—Ulyana's dialect—word by borrowed word. Her POV establishes her practiced invisibility and the estate agent's cheerful pressure to finish fast. Emotional beat: grief deferred, a woman fluent in everyone's language but her own heart.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Clearing Ulyana's bedroom, she finds a loose panel and a tin box of unsent postcards, dated across four decades, addressed to a sister named Lida and to her own mother. The first one she reads stops her breath. Emotional beat: the past breaks through the wallpaper; the sale deadline begins ticking.

chapters.title: A Grammar of Silence
chapters.summary: Freya begins translating the earliest postcards, relearning the dialect as she goes, and visits the town archive where librarian Tomas—a warm, persistent local—offers help she keeps refusing. She learns Lida died at nineteen, before most of the letters were even written. Emotional beat: the ache of translating words meant for no one.

chapters.title: The Partner's Name
chapters.summary: Middle-era postcards reveal Ulyana's husband and his business partner, Aurel Kovac, whose name is struck from every later letter. Freya's mother, a girl in the background of the letters, begins to emerge as the family's truth-teller. Emotional beat: the discovery that the family fortune has a wound at its center.

chapters.title: What Mother Knew
chapters.summary: Freya calls her estranged mother, Ingrid, and gets three minutes of frost before the line goes dead. In a flashback chapter from Ulyana's postcard-voice, we learn Ingrid was exiled after confronting Ulyana about Aurel. Freya realizes her own silence was inherited. Emotional beat: the recognition that she has become her grandmother.

chapters.title: The Buyer's Deadline
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. The buyer's lawyer demands early completion; the estate agent pushes; Tomas, sorting postcards with her, gently asks why she's really hiding them. A descendant of Aurel Kovac turns out to live in town. Emotional beat: loyalty to the dead pressing down like a closing door.

chapters.title: Kovac's Granddaughter
chapters.summary: Freya meets Mara Kovac at the harbor café and says nothing about the letters, but Mara mentions the family shame her grandfather carried to his grave. Guilt and temptation war in Freya: the truth could heal two families or detonate both. Emotional beat: the first honest conversation she's had in years, built on a lie of omission.

chapters.title: The Last Postcard
chapters.summary: Freya finds the final postcard, written in Ulyana's last year, addressed to Freya herself: an apology in the dying dialect, asking forgiveness for the silence that cost Ingrid and, eventually, Freya. She breaks down alone in the empty kitchen. Emotional beat: the climax of grief—the dead speaking directly at last.

chapters.title: Saying It Out Loud
chapters.summary: On the morning of the sale, Freya stands in the empty doorway and reads the final postcard aloud in Ulyana's language, then telephones Ingrid and reads it to her too. Her mother weeps, then goes quiet, then asks her to visit. Freya hands the box to Mara Kovac. Emotional beat: truth chosen over loyalty; goodbye said properly.

chapters.title: Borrowed No Longer
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Freya's POV from Ingrid's kitchen, then Vellamouth again: Mara has framed the Kovac letters in the town library; Tomas writes to her; Freya translates her first novel into Ulyana's dialect, restoring words she'd lost. The house is sold; the language is coming back. Emotional beat: found family, reclaimed voice, an ending that opens outward.
